title: The ballad in Majh
hookLine: Guru Nanak's Var in Majh with saloks (ang 137–150)
tomorrow: The dark age is a knife

lines: A SINGER, A DRUM, TWO FIGHTERS.
cards: A singer at a village fair, a drum, and a story of two fighters, sung verse after verse while the crowd leans in. Tradition says that's what a var was in the Punjab: a ballad of heroes and battles, sung loud.

Now open the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Majh, and there's a var by Guru Nanak, with a heading naming the tune it's sung to, after two figures from a ballad. Same drum, same shape. But the battle inside is a different kind.

teach.b: Start with the shape. A var in the Granth is built from pauris, stanzas, and some readers hear in pauri the word for a step, as on a ladder; each pauri moves the ballad up one rung.
Between them sit saloks, short verses that set up or answer each step. In Majh ki Var, some saloks carry Guru Nanak's name and some Guru Angad's, so two Gurus' voices meet in one ballad.

teach.h: SUNG TO A FOLK BALLAD'S TUNE.
teach.b: Next, the tune. The heading says to sing it to the tune of Malik Murid and Chandrahara Sohia. Tradition remembers them as heroes of a folk ballad, a song people already knew.
So the Guru took a sound the crowd could hum and filled it with something new. Then the opening. Before any battle, the first salok is about the Guru.
In plain English, not word for word: the Guru is the giver. The Guru is a house of ice, a cool place in the heat.
The Guru is the lamp of the three worlds, a gift that never runs out, and the one whose mind trusts the Guru finds peace.
Giver, coolness, lamp: after a week of burning summers and dark rainy nights, this ballad opens with shade and light.
And where a war song might open by praising a hero, this one praises the Guru, the one who shows the way. The fights that follow are inner ones: with ego, with falsehood, with a broken age.
That's today's line: the majh ballad.

how: Majh ki Var is sung in kirtan and read as part of the Guru Granth Sahib; in a var, the saloks and pauris are sung or read together, the salok first and then the pauri.

games.q: what does “the ballad in majh” mean?
o: a war hymn sung before battles in the Majh country
a folk song of two heroes, copied into scripture
Guru Nanak's var: a ballad of steps about inner battles

games.q: what's inside the ballad — tap the pairs.
p: a stanza; a step on a ladder
a short verse between the steps

s: Majh ki Var opens by praising a warrior hero
its first salok praises the Guru: giver, a house of ice, the lamp of the three worlds.
the heading names a tune to sing it to
it's to be sung to the tune of Malik Murid and Chandrahara Sohia.
all the saloks in Majh ki Var carry Guru Nanak's name
some carry Guru Nanak's name and some Guru Angad's.

games.q: you're setting a song about the inner life to music. what does the heading of Majh ki Var show Guru Nanak's ballad using?
o: a brand-new tune no one knew.
the tune of a folk ballad people already knew.
games.why: the heading names the tune of Malik Murid and Chandrahara Sohia: a familiar sound, filled with a new battle.

practice: If you can, play the opening of Majh ki Var, sung or recited; if not, sit with its three pictures. Breathe in: giver; breathe out: a cool house of ice; breathe in: a lamp, letting each one rest a few breaths.
Notice which one you need most today, and if you pray, say Waheguru beside it.

wordCard.voice: The ballad in Majh. Guru Nanak's var, a ballad in steps called pauris, with saloks between them, sung to an old ballad's tune and opening with the Guru as giver, coolness and lamp. Today's word.

orig.note: var: a ballad, the form of Guru Nanak's long poem in Majh.

carryVoice: Your line: the majh ballad. A ballad's drum, and a battle fought inside. See you tomorrow.
